source.title: Robustness of Adaptive Neural Network Optimization Under Training Noise

record.tranche_reason: The paper compares optimizers using noisy training data and clean test data. That shifted-distribution setting is outside the claim's same-distribution generalization scope. Its qualitative loss-surface analysis also does not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.gate_note: The results concern robustness to training perturbations: noisy training images are evaluated on clean test images. These are reported under fits_no_version, not mapped to the same-distribution versions. The paper also cites prior work on generalization; cited results are not rows.
record.test_reason: The image experiments test V4 in a new setting: noisy training images and clean held-out images. They compare adaptive optimizers with SGD and NAG under default learning rates and learning-rate sweeps. V4 does not require identical training and test distributions; the distribution shift qualifies the setting rather than excluding these results.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the authors' conclusion: SGD-based methods are more robust than adaptive methods to the tested training perturbations. Their explanation involving steep minima, spurious features, and diminishing updates is a proposed mechanism supported by qualitative analysis, rather than an established causal result.
record.recipe_differences: Studies optimizer robustness to crafted or common training perturbations, evaluating on clean data; it does not test the same-distribution generalization claims or interventions in the mapped versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset, optimizer, perturbation severity, learning rate, and the optimizer used internally during CMA-ES noise generation change reported outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: On synthetic linearly separable data, perturbed training leads adaptive methods to predict every clean test example as positive, while SGD and NAG classify perfectly; all optimizers show convergent test loss with clean training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer choice can determine robustness to spurious training features in synthetic linear classification.

fits_no_version.finding: Qualitative two-dimensional loss plots show steeper solutions for Adam than SGD, with Adam's steepness increasing with noise severity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Qualitative local loss geometry differs between optimizers under training noise.

record.problems: Most image-dataset comparisons are shown in figures without numeric values in the text. The paper reports means of three runs for its displayed experiments but supplies no uncertainty estimates. The ImageNet attacks are explicitly approximate and use a subsampled 10-class dataset. The results concern noisy training data and clean test data.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Many figure-only optimizer-by-dataset accuracy traces are not entered as separate rows when the text does not describe their distinct outcomes; see Figures 3–6 and 9–20. The text gives qualitative comparisons for those plots, captured where stated in the rows and fits_no_version.

untested.parts: Fixed random-label fitting versus natural-label held-out accuracy using the same architecture and recipe.
Width sweeps beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the contribution of local connectivity.
Language benchmarks, systematic broad hyperparameter tuning, decoupled weight decay, switching optimizers, and unperturbed image-benchmark comparisons.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and compensating training recipes.
Dropout interventions and their interactions with dataset size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, quantitative ranking of generalization gaps, and comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removal of memorized examples versus matched random removal.

missing.what: Training accuracy is reported as reaching 100% in most worst-case-noise experiments, and nearly 100% in most convergent learning-rate conditions. Record this qualification alongside held-out results to assess whether optimizer differences persist despite comparable training performance.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for any version. Class-specific input perturbations create the tested setting; they do not directly prescribe which optimizer must generalize worse. Common impulse noise and noise optimized internally against SGD also favor SGD-based methods in the supplied text. Those figure-based comparisons are already declared in rows_left_out. Numerical figure values cannot be reconstructed from the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization under the same distribution.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and their effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks on images.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization on natural training and held-out data from the same distribution; language benchmarks and the tuning or recipe qualifications in the version.
Large-batch versus small-batch training under fixed epoch budgets.
The effect of dropout and its interaction with training-set size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation sharpness, its association with the training-test gap, and comparisons against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.

relationships.condition: Custom CNNs trained on pixel-perturbed MNIST, CIFAR10, and SVHN with default optimizer learning rates
relationships.reason: R9–R17 establish worse held-out performance for adaptive methods; MNIST yields Adam 43% and RMSProp 55% versus SGD 78% and NAG 74%.
relationships.display_finding: Reported held-out performance favored SGD-based methods over adaptive optimizers on perturbed images, but these comparisons remain unverified.

relationships.condition: Ten-class ImageNet subset with lower-intensity approximate attacks, AMSGrad versus NAG
relationships.reason: R18–R19 report identical 93.6% accuracy, showing that the adaptive disadvantage depends on optimizer and noise condition.
relationships.display_finding: Reported identical accuracy of 93.6% for AMSGrad and NAG remains unverified.

relationships.condition: Ten-class ImageNet subset with higher-intensity approximate attacks
relationships.reason: R20 explicitly reports that SGD and NAG outperform adaptive methods, although numerical differences are unavailable.
relationships.display_finding: Reported performance favored SGD and NAG over adaptive methods, but exact differences were unavailable and the comparison remains unverified.

relationships.condition: MNIST ResNet18 and ResNet50 experiments with learning-rate sweeps
relationships.reason: R27–R28 and Section VII-E explicitly report greater robustness for SGD-based methods after testing learning rates from 0.1 to 0.0001.
relationships.display_finding: Reported robustness favored SGD-based methods after learning-rate sweeps, but these comparisons remain unverified.
